purpose: Customer-safe guide evidence map for novice/customer-surface evals. It proves whether a guide has authored text, a stable article id/alias, and screenshot-backed visual evidence without exposing test ids, asset ids, or source paths.

guides.name: Create an onboarding
guides.userNeed: Start one V2 onboarding draft from this page; avoid duplicate drafts for the same campaign.

sections.title: Start from the onboarding list
sections.description: Click Create Onboarding to open the setup wizard. It walks you through three things in order: naming the draft, choosing where it will be published (pick Web if you're building an ad landing page), and picking a starting theme. After that the draft opens on the canvas ready to edit.

sections.title: Name and organize the draft
sections.description: Give the draft a clear internal name — this is just for you to find it in the list, and visitors never see it. Optionally drop it in a folder to keep a long list tidy. Keep one draft per ad campaign instead of making duplicates, because separate drafts split your analytics and make results harder to read.

guides.name: Onboarding wizard: basic information
guides.userNeed: Set name, platform, and language first — platform controls the publish surface and runtime behavior.

sections.title: Name the onboarding
sections.description: Use a clear internal name so the draft is easy to find in the Onboardings list. The name is not shown to visitors.

sections.title: Choose the platform
sections.description: The platform controls the publish surface and runtime behavior. Web flows publish through Web Placement; pick it before selecting a theme.

sections.title: Set the default language
sections.description: The default language is the fallback locale used when a visitor has no matching localized content. Choose the primary audience language.

sections.title: Add supported languages
sections.description: Add every locale you intend to publish so screens can carry localized copy from the start. You can extend this later, but planning it now avoids rework.

sections.title: Optionally assign a folder
sections.description: Choose a folder to organize the draft in the Onboardings list, or leave it at the root level. The folder only affects organization and can be changed later.

guides.name: Onboarding wizard: theme selection
guides.userNeed: Pick a theme that covers all planned screen types, not just the first screen.

sections.title: Pick the visual baseline
sections.description: Click a theme card to set it as the baseline for colors, fonts, spacing, and screen layouts. The selected card is highlighted and becomes the starting point for the Customize step.

sections.title: Keep it reusable
sections.description: Prefer a theme that can cover every planned screen type rather than optimizing only for the first screen. You can fine-tune everything in the next step.

guides.name: Onboarding wizard: theme customization
guides.userNeed: Tune high-level theme settings now; do screen-specific copy/layout later in the Screen Editor.

sections.title: Set the color scheme
sections.description: Three color pickers define the whole theme. Button Background fills the color behind your buttons, Titles & Subtitles sets the color of heading text (subtitles automatically reuse it at half opacity for a softer, secondary look), and Button Title sets the text color inside buttons. These colors carry into every screen you create, so set them once here.

sections.title: Choose fonts and text styling
sections.description: Main Font Family is the base font used for all text. You can give Titles and Subtitles their own family, weight, size, color, and alignment if you want them to stand out. Your font choices flow into option cards, product cards, and every screen, so this is what sets the overall voice and feel of the funnel.

sections.title: Style the option and product cards
sections.description: These controls style the tappable cards visitors choose from. Checkbox Kind sets circle or square selection markers, List Border Radius rounds the card corners (0 = sharp, 32 = very rounded; around 12 looks modern), and Item Title and Item Subtitle set the text inside each card. They apply to list, grid, and paywall product screens — anywhere a visitor makes a choice.

sections.title: Set the background
sections.description: Choose a solid color, a photo, or a video clip to sit behind every screen. Whatever you pick must keep headings, body text, and buttons easy to read — low contrast here hurts conversion on every single screen, so favor a calm background over a busy one.

sections.title: Configure the header bar
sections.description: The header bar sits at the top of every screen. Toggle the back button, the skip button, and the progress indicator on or off. Leaving the progress indicator on reassures visitors how far along they are, which helps them finish; colors and fonts here inherit from your theme automatically.

sections.title: Configure the action buttons
sections.description: These are the buttons at the bottom of each screen — a primary one (usually 'Continue') and an optional secondary one. Set whether each is shown, its label style, and its look. Their colors pull from your Titles & Subtitles and Button Title theme colors, so they stay consistent across all screens without per-screen tweaks.

sections.title: Review the live preview
sections.description: The carousel on the left shows sample screens using your current settings, updating in real time as you change them. Use it to confirm text is readable and spacing looks right before you commit — fixing the theme now is far faster than editing every screen one by one afterward.

sections.title: Create the onboarding
sections.description: Click Create to apply this theme and generate the draft. Everything you set here is just a starting point — you can still override the colors, fonts, and layout on any individual screen later in the Screen Editor.

guides.name: Custom Domain setup
guides.userNeed: Decide whether to use a branded custom domain and know the order: enter domain, set DNS, verify, then publish.

sections.title: Why a custom domain matters
sections.description: A custom domain (for example funnel.example.com) swaps the generic Segmently link for your own brand. A branded link looks more trustworthy in ads and emails, so more people click and fewer drop off before reaching your funnel. It's optional — publishing still works fine on the default Segmently domain if you skip it.

sections.title: Recommended order of steps
sections.description: Work through it in this order: (1) enter your domain, (2) add the DNS records Segmently shows you at your domain provider, (3) click Verify and wait for the 'Verified' status, then (4) select that verified domain when you publish a Web Placement. Verification has to succeed before the domain can serve your live funnel, so don't publish against it until the status is green.

guides.name: Custom Domain: domain input
guides.userNeed: Enter the exact public host (no protocol/path) and confirm the owner can edit DNS.

sections.title: Enter the public host visitors will open
sections.description: Type the exact address visitors will see in the link, such as funnel.example.com. A subdomain like funnel. is recommended and the easiest to verify — a bare root domain (example.com with no prefix) is harder to set up and not all providers support it. Enter only the hostname: no https://, no slashes, no path, and no query string.

sections.title: Before you save
sections.description: Make sure you — or whoever controls this domain — can edit its DNS records, because the very next step asks you to add records at the domain provider. Verification can't finish until those records are live, so don't save until you know you have that access.

guides.name: Custom Domain: DNS setup
guides.userNeed: Apply the provided DNS records exactly (DNS-only, no proxy) and wait for propagation before verifying.

sections.title: Add the DNS records at your provider
sections.description: Copy each DNS record shown in the table here into your domain provider's DNS settings exactly as displayed — the record type, the name/host, and the value all have to match. After you save them at the provider, wait before verifying: DNS changes take from a few minutes up to a few hours to spread across the internet, and verification only passes once they're live.

sections.title: If verification keeps failing
sections.description: First, remove any older CNAME or A record on the same host that conflicts with the new one. Second, if your domain is on Cloudflare, set the record to 'DNS only' — click the orange cloud icon so it turns grey. The orange cloud means Cloudflare is hiding (proxying) your real record, which stops Segmently from confirming it.

guides.name: Custom Domain: verification
guides.userNeed: Verify the domain (retry after DNS propagates) so the published funnel can serve from the branded URL.

sections.title: Verify before you publish
sections.description: Click Verify and Segmently checks the DNS records you added at your domain provider. The domain has to reach a 'Verified' status before it can reliably serve your live funnel. If it shows 'Failed' or 'Pending', don't re-enter the records — DNS changes take time to spread across the internet (usually minutes, sometimes a few hours). Just wait and click Verify again.

sections.title: What a verified domain unlocks
sections.description: Once the status turns to 'Verified', the domain becomes selectable as the destination when you publish a Web Placement. Your live funnel link then carries your own brand (for example funnel.example.com) instead of the default Segmently address — which looks more trustworthy in ads and emails and tends to lift click-through.

guides.name: Stripe Connect setup
guides.userNeed: Know that Stripe must be connected before paywall products can map to Stripe prices, and where that connection lives.

sections.title: Connect Stripe before adding products
sections.description: Click Connect to link your Stripe account here first — Segmently needs it to match each paywall product to a real Stripe product and price so payments actually go through. Stripe's Test and Live environments are separate accounts, so each needs its own connection. Start with Test mode so you can run a full checkout safely before any real money moves.

sections.title: Custom deployment? Register OAuth redirect URLs first (one-time)
sections.description: You only need this if your team runs a custom or self-hosted Segmently install. In that case an admin must add the OAuth callback URL in the Stripe Dashboard (Connect Settings) before the Connect button will work, because Stripe rejects an unregistered redirect URL. On the standard hosted Segmently this is already handled for you — you can skip this step.

guides.name: Stripe Connect: test mode
guides.userNeed: Connect test mode first to validate the paywall and checkout safely before charging real customers.

sections.title: Connect a test Stripe account
sections.description: Use Connect Test Account to authorize Segmently for your test Stripe account. Test mode uses sandbox cards (for example 4242 4242 4242 4242) and never charges real customers, so validate products and checkout here first.

sections.title: Check the test account status
sections.description: After connecting, confirm the account shows charges enabled. If onboarding is incomplete, finish it in the Stripe Dashboard; you cannot create products or test checkout until charges are enabled.

guides.name: Stripe Connect: live mode
guides.userNeed: Connect live mode to the production Stripe account only when real products, prices, and payouts are ready.

sections.title: Connect your live Stripe account
sections.description: Use Connect Live Account to authorize your production account. Live mode processes real payments and maps to your production products and prices, so connect it only after test validation is complete.

sections.title: Verify live account readiness
sections.description: Confirm that both charges and payouts are enabled before deploying a paywall to production. Finish any remaining business verification (identity, bank account) in the Stripe Dashboard if onboarding is incomplete.

sections.title: Keep test and live separate
sections.description: Test and live modes are independent and cannot be mixed in one published funnel. Every product in a single publish must use the same mode, so review the product mode before publishing to production.

guides.name: Stripe Connect: OAuth guidance
guides.userNeed: Authorize the correct Stripe mode so product/price lookup and checkout creation succeed for the published funnel.

sections.title: Why test and live need separate connections
sections.description: Stripe Connect Standard accounts require separate OAuth connections for test and live because each mode has its own account ID and API keys. This is a Stripe limitation; connecting test first is the recommended safe pattern.

sections.title: Know what you are granting
sections.description: OAuth authorizes Segmently to read your products and prices and to create new ones inline in the product dialog. You are not granting direct charge access; all charges run through your connected Stripe account.

sections.title: If products do not appear
sections.description: If your Stripe products or prices are missing in the picker, verify you selected the matching mode and that the products exist in that Stripe account, since test and live are separate catalogs. Refresh the page or reconnect OAuth if needed.

guides.name: Analytics setup
guides.userNeed: Configure analytics before traffic so visits, screen events, and checkout transitions are measured from the first run.

sections.title: Track the funnel before scaling
sections.description: Set up and verify analytics before publishing to traffic. Events are measured from the first visitor, so a destination added later cannot capture earlier sessions.

sections.title: Choose the provider, then verify
sections.description: Pick the analytics platform that matches your reporting workflow, then publish a test funnel and confirm events arrive in that provider dashboard within seconds.

sections.title: Enable GDPR consent management (optional)
sections.description: Toggle consent management to show a consent banner in regulated regions. You set the default consent state, banner text, and privacy policy URL, and consent decisions gate which events are collected.

guides.name: Analytics integration list
guides.userNeed: Review which destinations are active and remove stale ones before validating events.

sections.title: Review active destinations
sections.description: This list shows every configured destination and whether it is enabled. Each enabled integration injects automatically into every published web funnel.

sections.title: Disable or remove stale destinations
sections.description: Before testing, turn off destinations that are no longer needed or use outdated tracking IDs. This keeps validation results clean and avoids polluting old analytics accounts.

sections.title: Enable Segmently Analytics (internal reporting)
sections.description: Segmently Analytics is the first-party provider behind Segmently Reports and canvas insights. Add and enable it to collect funnel events for reporting and optimization; it is disabled by default.

guides.name: Analytics: add provider
guides.userNeed: Add the analytics provider/endpoint the project reports through.

sections.title: Add a destination
sections.description: Use Add to open the provider picker, then choose from 15+ client and server platforms (Amplitude, GA4, GTM, Mixpanel, PostHog, Facebook Pixel, TikTok Pixel, custom scripts, and server-side variants).

sections.title: Publish and verify
sections.description: After saving, publish a test Web Placement and watch the provider dashboard for incoming events (page views, screen changes, actions, checkout steps). If nothing arrives within 30 seconds, recheck the ID or token.

guides.name: Analytics provider configuration
guides.userNeed: Enter the provider-specific id/token correctly, then verify events arrive before relying on the data.

sections.title: Name the integration
sections.description: Enter a clear label such as 'GA4 Production' or 'Amplitude EU'. It only appears in your own integrations list and edit menus to help you tell destinations apart — visitors never see it. Pick a name that says which tool and which environment it points at.

sections.title: Google Analytics 4: Measurement ID
sections.description: Paste your Measurement ID (it looks like G-XXXXXXXXXX). Find it in GA4 under Admin then Data Streams then your web stream. It routes every funnel event to the correct GA4 property; if the format is wrong, Segmently blocks the save so a typo can't silently break tracking.

sections.title: Amplitude: API key and server zone
sections.description: Paste the API Key from your Amplitude project Settings, then pick the server zone (US, or EU for GDPR data residency) that matches where your Amplitude project lives — the wrong zone means events never arrive. You can also turn on session start/end tracking to capture session lifecycle events.

sections.title: Google Tag Manager: Container ID
sections.description: Paste your Container ID (it looks like GTM-XXXXX) from Google Tag Manager. Segmently pushes every funnel event into the dataLayer, so your existing GTM triggers and tags fire on them. Only set a custom Data Layer name if your container was specifically built to expect a non-default one.

sections.title: Mixpanel: project token
sections.description: Paste the Project Token from your Mixpanel project Settings, then choose where it's stored on the visitor's browser (localStorage by default, or Cookie if your setup needs it). You can also enable page-view tracking if you want each screen view recorded automatically.

sections.title: PostHog: project token and region
sections.description: Paste the Project Token — that's the API key, not the numeric Project ID — found in PostHog under Settings then General. Then pick your region: US Cloud, EU Cloud, or Self-Hosted. If you chose Self-Hosted, also enter your own PostHog API host URL so events know where to go.

sections.title: Facebook (Meta) Pixel: Pixel ID
sections.description: Paste the Pixel ID from Meta Events Manager so your funnel and checkout events attribute back to your Facebook and Instagram ad campaigns. Optionally turn on auto-config to also capture button clicks and page metadata without extra setup.

sections.title: TikTok Pixel: Pixel ID
sections.description: Paste the Pixel ID (it looks like CXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX) from TikTok Ads Manager under Events. Under Advanced Matching you can optionally pass hashed email and phone, which improves how reliably TikTok attributes conversions back to your ads.

sections.title: Custom Script: HEAD and BODY
sections.description: For tools without a built-in option, add your own JavaScript at two points: code in HEAD runs before the page renders (load SDKs here), and code in BODY runs after it loads (attach handlers here). Call window.segmentlySDK.setCustomData(key, value) to hand funnel data to your script. Reach for this only when no built-in provider above fits.

sections.title: Server-side analytics (Conversions API, GA4 Measurement Protocol, and more)
sections.description: Server-side destinations send payment events straight from Segmently's servers — purchase, subscription, cancellation, and failure only — for revenue attribution that ad-blockers and browser limits can't drop. They use the same credentials as the matching client pixel but do not receive engagement events (screen views, button taps), so run them alongside the client pixel to track the full funnel.

guides.name: Paywall Products list
guides.userNeed: Create products here before attaching them to a paywall screen; they must match the Stripe mode the funnel publishes in.

sections.title: Create products before attaching them
sections.description: Paywall screens can only sell products that exist here, and every product must match the Stripe mode of the published flow. Create, edit, and delete products from this page.

sections.title: Keep test and live separate
sections.description: Use test products for sandbox flows and live products for production flows. Mixing modes is the most common reason checkout setup fails.

guides.name: Paywall Products mode tabs
guides.userNeed: Pick the Test/Live tab that matches the Stripe connection and the funnel you will publish, to avoid checkout mode mismatches.

sections.title: Switch between Test and Live catalogs
sections.description: The Test and Live tabs hold two completely separate product catalogs, each with its own count badge. Start in Test while you're still validating — it can't charge real cards. Always glance at which tab is selected before you create or edit a product, so it lands in the right catalog.

sections.title: Keep the mode consistent everywhere
sections.description: A product only works at checkout if the paywall screen, your Stripe connection, and this tab are all in the same mode. A real launch needs a Live product with a Live Stripe connection; a safe rehearsal needs a Test product with a Test connection. Mixing modes is the most common reason a paywall fails to charge.

guides.name: Paywall Product: basic fields
guides.userNeed: Define product name, type, and checkout behavior so the offer appears and creates checkout correctly.

sections.title: Select Stripe mode
sections.description: Choose whether this product uses your Test or Live Stripe credentials. Test mode lets you rehearse the whole checkout with no real charge; Live charges real customers. It has to match your connected Stripe mode and the mode you publish in — if they don't line up, checkout will fail.

sections.title: Choose the checkout experience
sections.description: Pick how the payment form appears. An embedded form slides up as a bottom sheet and keeps visitors inside your funnel — recommended for most funnels since staying in-flow converts better. A full-page Stripe Checkout redirect is simpler to set up but sends the visitor away to Stripe's own hosted page.

sections.title: Name the product
sections.description: Set the display name customers see on the paywall and at checkout — this field is required. Use clear, benefit-focused wording like 'Premium Annual Plan' rather than an internal code or SKU, since this is part of the buying decision.

sections.title: Add a description (optional)
sections.description: Optionally add supporting text shown on the paywall and inside the Studio to spell out what's included, the key benefits, or the terms. Leave it blank if the product name already says everything a buyer needs to know.

sections.title: Choose the product type
sections.description: Select subscription (recurring, billed on a schedule) or one-time payment (charged once). This decides which trial and subscription options appear below and which Stripe prices are eligible. If you change it after a live product is already wired up, retest checkout before you relaunch.

guides.name: Paywall Product: Stripe mapping
guides.userNeed: Map the product to the right Stripe product/price (same account mode) so checkout charges the intended amount.

sections.title: Select or create the Stripe product
sections.description: Link this paywall product to a real product in your Stripe account, or click to create one inline without leaving this dialog. It has to live in the same Stripe mode (Test or Live) you selected above — if it's in the other mode it won't show up in the list.

sections.title: Select or create the Stripe price
sections.description: Pick the exact price customers will be charged — this is what actually drives checkout, so if you leave the price empty the paywall will fail when a visitor tries to pay. The list filters to recurring prices for subscriptions and one-time prices for single purchases; if none fits, create a new price inline.

guides.name: Paywall Product: price setup
guides.userNeed: Set amount, currency, and recurrence to the exact values customers should see at checkout.

sections.title: Set the amount and primary currency
sections.description: Enter the base price and currency (USD, EUR, GBP, RUB) customers are charged at checkout. Type it in whole currency units — enter 9.99 for nine dollars ninety-nine, not 999. This value is sent to Stripe and shown to customers, so double-check it before you publish.

sections.title: Set the price type and recurrence
sections.description: Choose one-time (charged once) or recurring (billed on a schedule). For recurring, set the interval (day, week, month, year) and the count: count 1 bills every period, count 3 bills every third period — so interval 'month' + count 3 equals quarterly billing.

sections.title: Add optional multi-currency pricing
sections.description: Optionally add up to five extra currencies with their own amounts so international visitors see prices in their local money, which lifts conversion. At checkout Segmently shows the local price when one is defined for the visitor's currency; otherwise it falls back to your primary currency above.

guides.name: Paywall Product: subscription options
guides.userNeed: Configure billing interval and trial so the subscription matches the Stripe price and the paywall copy.

sections.title: Set the billing interval
sections.description: Choose how often customers are billed (daily, weekly, monthly, yearly) and the Every-X count for multi-period billing — for example every 3 months. This has to match the recurrence on the Stripe price you mapped, or Stripe will reject the checkout.

sections.title: Configure the free trial
sections.description: Set how many free days a customer gets before the first charge; enter 0 for no trial. Billing starts the day after the trial ends. Always state the trial length clearly on the paywall — it keeps checkout compliant and cuts down on disputes and chargebacks from surprised customers.

sections.title: Charge an upfront fee at sign-up (optional)
sections.description: Turn this on to charge a one-time fee the moment the subscription starts, on top of the recurring price — useful for an activation or onboarding fee. Leave it off for a standard free-trial or pay-as-you-go subscription. (This is what the 'paid trial' setting controls: an immediate charge, not a free period.)

sections.title: Select the upfront fee price
sections.description: Pick or create the one-time Stripe price used for that upfront fee. It's charged immediately and billed separately from the recurring subscription, so it shows up as its own line in Stripe.

guides.name: V2 canvas overview
guides.userNeed: Read the flow on the canvas to confirm the route, the launch screen, and that paywall screens point to valid products before publish.

sections.title: Read the flow structure
sections.description: The canvas shows every screen as a node and every transition as an edge. Drag to arrange, click to select, and double-click a node to open the Screen Editor; the flow runs left to right.

sections.title: Identify the launch screen
sections.description: The first screen carries a First screen label on its left. The launch screen is where every visitor enters; only one can be the launch screen and it cannot have incoming connections.

sections.title: Use the toolbar controls
sections.description: The top bar has undo, redo, and close; the side panel has search, a locale selector when multiple languages exist, and a funnel-insights toggle. Shortcuts: Ctrl+Z undo, Ctrl+Shift+Z redo, Ctrl+F search.

sections.title: Navigate the canvas
sections.description: Scroll to zoom, hold space and drag to pan, and use the minimap in the corner for the full layout. Click to select a screen; Ctrl+click to multi-select.

guides.name: V2 canvas: add screen
guides.userNeed: Add the screen type the flow needs (question/content/embed/paywall) from the template panel, then edit its sections.

sections.title: Open the Screen Templates panel
sections.description: The right sidebar lists draggable screen templates with previews and is always visible. It is the primary way to add new screens to the canvas.

sections.title: Search for a screen type
sections.description: Type to filter templates by name or description; the list updates as you type. Clear the field to see all templates.

sections.title: Drag a template onto the canvas
sections.description: Click and hold a template, then drop it on the canvas to add the screen. Double-click the new node to open the Screen Editor and configure it.

sections.title: Choose screen types intentionally
sections.description: Question screens collect answers into variables for routing, content screens explain value, embed screens host custom HTML, and paywall screens sell products. Pick by what each step should accomplish.

sections.title: Screen names stay unique automatically
sections.description: When you add a screen whose type already exists, the system appends a number (for example Hero Content 2). This keeps analytics and navigation unambiguous.

guides.name: V2 canvas: connect screens
guides.userNeed: Connect screens so each action leads to the right next screen; verify default and conditional paths.

sections.title: Find the connection ports
sections.description: Each node has handles on its edges: input handles on the left of non-launch screens, and one output handle per action on the right. Hover a handle to see its action label.

sections.title: Draw a default connection
sections.description: Drag from an output handle on the source to an input handle on the target to create an edge. This is an unconditional path: every visitor who takes that action goes to the target.

sections.title: Add conditions to a connection
sections.description: Click an edge to open Connection Details, then Edit Conditions to define AND/OR logic on flow variables. Conditional paths activate only when the conditions are true.

sections.title: Remove a connection
sections.description: Click an edge, then Delete Connection and confirm. The target becomes unreachable through that action unless another path exists.

sections.title: Verify the flow is complete
sections.description: Before publishing, confirm a launch screen is set, every non-final screen has an outgoing connection, paywall screens point to valid products, and each branch ends meaningfully.

sections.title: FlexibleLayout sections add their own handles
sections.description: FlexibleLayout screens hold multiple sections (content, buttons, options, embeds, paywalls), and each can generate its own connection handles. Handles appear automatically based on the sections you add.

sections.title: Carousel and ProgressSteps auto-advance
sections.description: Carousel and ProgressSteps screens advance on a timer rather than a button, so their timer handle is what you route from. These types have no Action Bar because visitors do not click Continue.

guides.name: Screen Editor overview
guides.userNeed: Understand that copy, layout, media, variables, actions, and background for one screen are configured here, in shared and unique sections.

sections.title: Understand shared vs unique sections
sections.description: Shared sections (Header, Action Bar, Backdrop, Basic Config) repeat across screen types; unique sections like Media, Options, or Text Field appear only where the type needs them. Know which sections your screen exposes.

sections.title: Navigate the right panel
sections.description: The right panel is a set of collapsible sections in screen-type order. Expand each accordion to reach its controls; text, styles, translations, and behavior are grouped within their section.

sections.title: Work in the recommended order
sections.description: Configure top to bottom: Header, Content, Options or Media, Action Bar, Background, then Basic Config. This order follows the visitor flow from orientation to visual treatment.

sections.title: Bind variables on selection screens
sections.description: Selection screens (list, grid, text input, wheel picker) expose a Variable Binding section. Create or pick a flow variable, map items to options, and set score effects to influence later routing.

guides.name: Screen Editor action button
guides.userNeed: Set the action button label/behavior so the next step is clear and the canvas transition matches it; keep required inputs blocking.

sections.title: Set the primary button label
sections.description: The primary button text is the visible call-to-action (Continue, Next, Subscribe). Make it reflect the screen goal so visitors know what happens on click.

sections.title: Control primary button visibility
sections.description: Toggle the primary button on or off. Hide it when visitors must interact with the content first; at least one of the primary or secondary buttons must stay visible.

sections.title: Style the primary button
sections.description: Apply text and button styling through five accordion groups: Container (padding), Gradient, Shadow, Effects, and Icon. Strong styling makes the button read as the important next step.

sections.title: Add an optional secondary button
sections.description: Enable and label a secondary action (Skip, Learn More, Log In) for an alternative path. Keep it less prominent than the primary; use it for exits, not the main goal.

sections.title: Control secondary button visibility
sections.description: When the secondary button is enabled, toggle it visible or hidden. Hide it to force commitment to the primary action only.

sections.title: Style the secondary button
sections.description: Style the secondary button with the same five accordion groups but lower visual priority (softer colors, lighter weight) to preserve the hierarchy.

sections.title: Understand button layout
sections.description: Buttons stack vertically or horizontally based on width and theme, with the primary always before the secondary. Layout is automatic, so focus on labels and styling.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Header
guides.userNeed: Know what the Header section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Header section
sections.description: Controls the bar at the top of the screen: the Back and Skip buttons and the progress indicator that shows how far through the flow a visitor is. Most screens inherit sensible defaults — style the progress indicator (kind and colors) so it matches your brand.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: HeroContent, Carousel, ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, ProgressSteps, TextInput, WheelPicker, HeroList, WebEmbed.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Action Bar
guides.userNeed: Know what the Action Bar section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Action Bar section
sections.description: The Action Bar holds the screen's main call-to-action: the primary button (like Continue) and an optional secondary button. This is the control that actually moves visitors forward, so set its label to match what happens next and make sure it points to the same screen you connected on the canvas. It shows on most interactive screens; if a screen has no continuation button, add the next step from the canvas instead.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: HeroContent, ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, TextInput, WheelPicker, HeroList, WebEmbed.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Background
guides.userNeed: Know what the Background section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Background section
sections.description: Sets the full-screen backdrop behind everything on this screen — a solid color, a photo, or a looping video. It is the first thing a visitor sees, so match it to the theme and keep enough contrast for the header and buttons to stay readable.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: HeroContent, Carousel, ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, TextInput, WheelPicker, HeroList, WebEmbed, Paywall, FlexibleLayout.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Content
guides.userNeed: Know what the Content section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Content section
sections.description: The Content section holds the words on the screen: your headline, supporting text, or the question you ask the visitor. This is the copy that does the persuading, so write it like ad copy with one clear value proposition or one focused question per screen, and edit it before you touch colors or layout. It's available on most screens with editable text; media-only and pure paywall screens use their own copy areas instead.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: HeroContent, ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, TextInput, WheelPicker, HeroList.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Basic Config
guides.userNeed: Know what the Basic Config section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Basic Config section
sections.description: Behavior settings for this screen that do not change its visible copy: the entry animation, preferring cached assets, requesting a system permission, and an optional auto-advance countdown. Most screens can be left at their defaults — reach for these only for timed intros or permission prompts.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: HeroContent, ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, TextInput, WheelPicker, HeroList, WebEmbed, Paywall.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Media
guides.userNeed: Know what the Media section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Media section
sections.description: The Media section adds an image or video that supports the screen's message: a product shot, a before/after, or a short explainer clip. On a paid landing page strong visuals build trust and lift conversion, but keep them relevant so they reinforce the headline instead of distracting from the choice or button the visitor needs to act on. It shows on choice screens and the wheel picker; headline screens set their image inside the Content section instead.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, WheelPicker.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Options
guides.userNeed: Know what the Options section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Options section
sections.description: The Options section defines the answer choices, product cards, or tappable rows a visitor picks from on a selection screen. This is the core interaction that captures what the visitor wants, so pair it with Variable Binding to save each choice and use it to personalize copy and send the visitor toward the right paywall. If a screen has no Options section, it isn't a selection screen; add a list or grid screen from the canvas.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, HeroList.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Variable Binding
guides.userNeed: Know what the Variable Binding section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Variable Binding section
sections.description: Variable Binding saves what the visitor chooses or types on this screen as a named value you can reuse later. That saved value is what lets you personalize the funnel: send visitors down different paths based on their answer, segment them in analytics, and pass their details to your paywall and Stripe checkout. Without a binding the answer isn't stored and can't influence anything later, so it appears on every screen that collects an answer.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, TextInput, WheelPicker.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Text Field
guides.userNeed: Know what the Text Field section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Text Field section
sections.description: The Text Field section turns a screen into a question that collects a free-text answer such as a name, email, or goal. Set the placeholder hint, validation, and styling here; the answer is saved in a variable you can later use to branch the flow or personalize copy. Use it whenever the visitor should type an answer rather than pick from options — that captured input is what makes the screen gather usable data.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: TextInput.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Carousel
guides.userNeed: Know what the Carousel section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Carousel section
sections.description: Configures a Carousel screen — a set of slides (image plus optional text) that auto-advance on a timer to tell a quick visual story. Use it for a punchy intro, and keep slides few and fast so visitors reach the next step.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: Carousel.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Stepper
guides.userNeed: Know what the Stepper section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Stepper section
sections.description: The Stepper section builds an auto-advancing progress sequence — timed steps with a moving bar and a title, subtitle, description, and optional image for each step. Use it on 'analyzing' or 'building your plan' screens to hold attention while results are prepared, since that sense of progress lifts how many visitors reach the paywall. It only appears on progress-steps screens; add one from the canvas, then set the total duration and per-step copy here.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: ProgressSteps.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Roller
guides.userNeed: Know what the Roller section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Roller section
sections.description: The Roller section configures a spinning wheel picker that captures a visitor's choice — a date, age, size, or similar value — and saves it in a variable you can reuse for personalization or routing. Reach for it when an input has many ordered options that would be too many to show as buttons. It only appears on wheel-picker screens; add one from the canvas, then set the data type, wheels, and label styling here.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: WheelPicker.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Custom HTML
guides.userNeed: Know what the Custom HTML section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Custom HTML section
sections.description: The Custom HTML section lets you render your own HTML, CSS, and JavaScript inside a screen when none of the built-in sections fit the design you need. The content runs in an isolated frame and connects to the funnel so it can read data and trigger navigation. Reach for it only for fully custom screens like a Figma export or a bespoke widget — for standard text, buttons, lists, or paywalls use the native sections, which stay responsive and tracked, and always preview custom screens on a phone.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: WebEmbed.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Paywall Header
guides.userNeed: Know what the Paywall Header section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Paywall Header section
sections.description: The Paywall Header is the top strip of a paywall screen. Use it for the close (X) button and an optional 'Restore Purchases' label, and to style their color, position, and timing. Keep it minimal — a clear way to close plus restore is enough for an ad-ready paywall, since anything extra up here pulls attention away from the offer below. It only appears on paywall screens.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: Paywall.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Paywall Media
guides.userNeed: Know what the Paywall Media section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Paywall Media section
sections.description: The Paywall Media section is the featured image or video at the top of the paywall that visually sells the offer — a product shot, before/after, or short demo. Choose Image or Video and upload your asset, then check the preview so it reinforces the promise without pushing the plan cards and purchase button out of view on a phone. A relevant, high-quality visual builds trust, while an irrelevant one just wastes screen space.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: Paywall.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Paywall Body
guides.userNeed: Know what the Paywall Body section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Paywall Body section
sections.description: The Paywall Body is the persuasion area above the plan cards, where you write the title, subtitle, and feature bullets that explain why the offer is worth paying for. Keep the title to one clear benefit and use the bullets for proof like guarantees and what's included, since this copy is what lifts conversion before the visitor ever looks at the price. Edit it on any paywall screen, ideally after connecting Stripe so the benefits you promise match the plans on sale.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: Paywall.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Paywall Subscriptions
guides.userNeed: Know what the Paywall Subscriptions section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Paywall Subscriptions section
sections.description: The Paywall Subscriptions section is where you list the plans a visitor can buy. Each plan row is tied to a real product in your connected Stripe account, so the price and billing period shown here must match an actual Stripe product or checkout will fail. Add one row per plan, pre-select the option you most want sold (usually the annual or best-value plan) to boost conversion, and set this up after connecting Stripe and creating your products.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: Paywall.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Paywall Footer
guides.userNeed: Know what the Paywall Footer section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Paywall Footer section
sections.description: The Paywall Footer is the bottom action zone of a paywall and holds your single most important conversion control: the purchase/subscribe button, plus the auto-renew disclosure and legal links (Restore, Terms of Use, Privacy Policy). For an ad-ready paywall you must have a working purchase button and filled-in Terms and Privacy links, because ad networks and app stores reject paywalls without them. It only appears on paywall screens.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: Paywall.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Flexible Sections
guides.userNeed: Know what the Flexible Sections section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Flexible Sections section
sections.description: Builds a FlexibleLayout screen from stacked sections you arrange yourself, giving full control over the vertical order, sizing, and spacing of pieces (media, text, buttons). Use it when the standard screen types do not give you the layout you need.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: FlexibleLayout.

guides.name: Screen Editor: Sticky Container
guides.userNeed: Know what the Sticky Container section controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Sticky Container section
sections.description: The Sticky Container pins one call-to-action button to the bottom of the screen so it stays visible while the visitor scrolls long content. Turn it on for screens where the next-step or buy button would otherwise scroll out of view — long sales copy, feature lists, the paywall — because keeping the button always tappable is one of the simplest ways to lift click-through on paid traffic. Leave it off on short screens that fit without scrolling, where it just adds clutter.

sections.title: Where it appears
sections.description: Covered screen types: FlexibleLayout.

guides.name: Web Placement entry rules
guides.userNeed: Route visitors to the right entry screen by source value, and always keep a valid default entry path.

sections.title: Add an entry screen rule
sections.description: Open the form to create a routing rule. Each rule matches a URL parameter value and routes the visitor to a start screen; rules are checked top to bottom and the first match wins.

sections.title: Choose the URL parameter to match
sections.description: Select a parameter you defined in Sources. Its key is read from the incoming URL (for example utm_campaign) when the funnel loads.

sections.title: Specify the value to match
sections.description: Enter the exact value the parameter must have to trigger the rule. The match is case-sensitive (for example, enter summer for utm_campaign=summer).

sections.title: Choose the start screen
sections.description: Pick the V2 step where matching visitors land; it must exist in the selected onboarding version. Saved visitor progress overrides rules.

sections.title: Enable or disable the rule
sections.description: Toggle a rule active or inactive. Disabled rules are kept but skipped at load, which is useful for testing or temporary pauses.

sections.title: Remove a rule
sections.description: Delete a rule permanently; this cannot be undone. With no matching rule, the default start screen is used.

guides.name: Web Placement Stripe metadata
guides.userNeed: Carry stable funnel values (email/UTM) into Stripe checkout/webhooks via metadata mapping.

sections.title: Why attach metadata, and how to add one
sections.description: Attaching metadata stamps extra info onto each Stripe payment so you can see, right in your Stripe Dashboard and payout reports, which ad campaign, traffic source, or quiz answer produced the sale. Click Add and pick one of your defined parameters (a URL, Server, Variable, or Custom value you set up in Sources). Its key becomes a field on every PaymentIntent. Stripe allows up to 50 such keys.

sections.title: Choose which parameter to send
sections.description: Select from the parameters you've already defined in Sources. The parameter's internal key becomes the field name shown in Stripe, and every value is sent to Stripe as plain text (a string), even numbers.

sections.title: Review the metadata preview
sections.description: The JSON preview shows exactly how your chosen parameters will appear on the payment in Stripe. Check the field names and values here before saving, so your revenue reporting and reconciliation line up with the right campaign or source data.

sections.title: Remove a parameter
sections.description: Delete a mapping to stop sending that field to Stripe on future payments. This only removes the mapping on this screen — it does not delete or change the parameter definition itself over in Sources.

sections.title: Watch the keys limit
sections.description: A counter shows how many of Stripe's 50 metadata keys you've used. The Add button turns off once you hit the limit, so if you need room for a new field, remove a mapping you no longer need first.

guides.name: Web Placement publish URL
guides.userNeed: Publish, copy the URL, and smoke-test the full flow (and checkout/analytics) in a clean session before sending traffic.

sections.title: Find the Cloud URL
sections.description: This is the live public URL of the published funnel, using your custom domain when configured. Share it in ads, emails, and landing pages.

sections.title: Copy the URL
sections.description: Copy the Cloud URL to the clipboard for campaigns and links. The button shows a checkmark to confirm the copy.

sections.title: Open the funnel in a new tab
sections.description: Open the Cloud URL to confirm it loads before sending traffic. It runs with full analytics and Stripe checkout.

sections.title: Test locally with the Debug Panel (dev only)
sections.description: On localhost, a local URL with the Debug Panel shows live variable inspection, analytics preview, and error logs. Use it for QA before release.

sections.title: Complete a smoke test
sections.description: Open the Cloud URL in a clean (incognito) session, complete the flow, confirm analytics events fire, and test the paywall or checkout before sending traffic.

guides.name: Screen field: Back Button Label
guides.userNeed: Know what "Back Button Label" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Back Button Label
sections.description: Sets the text and styling of the Back control that returns visitors to the previous step. Defaults to a left arrow and supports other languages. Keep it small so it doesn't compete with your main action, and clear it to hide the button on the first screen, where there's nowhere to go back to.

guides.name: Screen field: Skip Button Label
guides.userNeed: Know what "Skip Button Label" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Skip Button Label
sections.description: Sets the text and styling of the Skip control that lets visitors bypass this step. Defaults to 'SKIP' and supports other languages. Use it only where skipping is fine, and clear it to hide it on your paywall and key question screens, where an easy out lowers both sales and the answers you collect.

guides.name: Screen field: Progress Bar Style
guides.userNeed: Know what "Progress Bar Style" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Progress Bar Style
sections.description: Chooses how progress through the funnel looks: a single continuous bar (Line) or segmented dots (Dashes), each with its own color controls below. A visible 'how far along' cue reassures visitors only a few steps remain, which lifts completion. Pick whichever fits your brand and keep it the same across screens.

guides.name: Screen field: Completed Progress Color
guides.userNeed: Know what "Completed Progress Color" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Completed Progress Color
sections.description: Colors the filled, completed part of the progress bar. Defaults to gold for the Line style and teal for Dashes. Use your brand accent and make sure it clearly stands out against the unfilled track color so visitors can see at a glance how far they've come.

guides.name: Screen field: Remaining Progress Color
guides.userNeed: Know what "Remaining Progress Color" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Remaining Progress Color
sections.description: Colors the empty, not-yet-completed part of the progress bar. Defaults to white for the Line style and light gray for Dashes. Keep it muted next to the filled color so the completed portion clearly reads as progress rather than blending in.

guides.name: Screen field: Progress Bar Text
guides.userNeed: Know what "Progress Bar Text" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Progress Bar Text
sections.description: Optional text shown with the progress bar, such as a 'Step 5 of 10' counter or a short line of reassurance. Supports other languages and styling; leave it empty for a clean bar-only look. Note this text is fixed per screen and won't count up on its own, so use it as a label unless you drive it from a variable.

guides.name: Screen field: Optional Header Icon
guides.userNeed: Know what "Optional Header Icon" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Optional Header Icon
sections.description: Adds an optional small icon, often a logo or step glyph, next to the progress bar, with controls for the image, its size, and its spacing. Most funnels leave this off. Use it only to reinforce branding in the header, and keep the icon small so it doesn't crowd the progress bar.

guides.name: Screen field: Progress Content Side
guides.userNeed: Know what "Progress Content Side" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Progress Content Side
sections.description: Sets where the icon and label sit across the header, on the left (Start), centered, or on the right (End). Mostly a cosmetic touch: centered usually looks balanced, while left or right lets you line the label up with your Back or Skip button. Adjust only if the default looks off.

guides.name: Screen field: Stretch Progress Edge-To-Edge
guides.userNeed: Know what "Stretch Progress Edge-To-Edge" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Stretch Progress Edge-To-Edge
sections.description: When on, the progress bar stretches all the way across the header; when off, it takes only the width its content needs. Use full width for a bold, obvious progress bar across the top of the screen. Turn it off when you want the bar compact and grouped with a label or icon.

guides.name: Screen field: Keep Progress Clear Of Buttons
guides.userNeed: Know what "Keep Progress Clear Of Buttons" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Keep Progress Clear Of Buttons
sections.description: When on, which is the default, the progress bar shrinks so it never overlaps the Back or Skip buttons; when off, it can collide with them in a tight header. Leave it on. Turn it off only if you've removed those buttons and want the bar to use the full width.

guides.name: Screen field: Progress Height In Header
guides.userNeed: Know what "Progress Height In Header" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Progress Height In Header
sections.description: Sets where the progress bar sits up and down within the header: at the top, centered, or at the bottom. Centered is the usual balanced choice; use bottom to sit it just above your content, or top to hug the status bar. Adjust only if the default placement looks off for your header height.

guides.name: Screen field: Header Bar Height
guides.userNeed: Know what "Header Bar Height" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Header Bar Height
sections.description: Sets how tall the header bar is, from 20 to 200 pixels, with a default of 44, which is the space its buttons and progress bar share. Keep it near the default for a standard bar and raise it only if you add a tall icon or larger text. Going too small cramps the Back and Skip buttons and makes them hard to tap.

guides.name: Screen field: Header Bar Background
guides.userNeed: Know what "Header Bar Background" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Header Bar Background
sections.description: Fills the header bar with a color, or clear it to transparent so the screen background shows through for a floating header. Use a solid color to set the header apart from busy content. If you go transparent over a photo or video, check that the Back, Skip, and progress colors still stand out clearly.

guides.name: Screen field: Header See-Through Level
guides.userNeed: Know what "Header See-Through Level" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Header See-Through Level
sections.description: Fades the whole header bar from fully solid to fully see-through, defaulting to solid. Lower it for a soft, partly transparent header that blends into a photo or video background. Keep it high enough that the Back, Skip, and progress controls stay easy to see.

guides.name: Screen field: Spacing inside the header
guides.userNeed: Know what "Spacing inside the header" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Spacing inside the header
sections.description: Sets the inner spacing on each side (top, right, bottom, left) that pushes the Back button, Skip button, and progress bar away from the header edges. Raise the top value to keep these controls clear of the phone's status bar or notch, and adjust left/right so buttons aren't jammed against the screen edge. Start from the defaults and nudge only where something looks cramped, since a clean header keeps the first impression of your ad landing page tidy.

guides.name: Screen field: Spacing around the progress bar
guides.userNeed: Know what "Spacing around the progress bar" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Spacing around the progress bar
sections.description: Sets the spacing on each side of the progress indicator alone, separate from the header's overall padding. Use it to fine-tune the gap around the bar, for example to nudge it down from the buttons, without moving the buttons themselves. Most funnels keep the default; adjust only when the bar sits too tight or too loose against the header.

guides.name: Screen field: Back button text style
guides.userNeed: Know what "Back button text style" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Back button text style
sections.description: Overrides how the Back control's label looks — font, size, weight, color, alignment, line height, an optional highlight behind the text, and a strikethrough color. By default it inherits your project theme, which keeps every screen consistent. Touch this only when the Back label needs to match a specific header treatment, and keep it subtle so it never competes with your main action.

guides.name: Screen field: Skip button text style
guides.userNeed: Know what "Skip button text style" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Skip button text style
sections.description: Overrides how the Skip control's label looks — font, size, weight, color, alignment, line height, an optional highlight, and a strikethrough color. By default it inherits your theme. Keep Skip visually quiet (smaller, lower-contrast) so it doesn't pull attention away from continuing; restyle it only to fit a specific header look.

guides.name: Screen field: Progress text style
guides.userNeed: Know what "Progress text style" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Progress text style
sections.description: Overrides how the progress label (for example 'Step 5 of 10') looks — font, size, weight, color, alignment, line height, an optional highlight, and a strikethrough color. By default it inherits your theme. Use it to make the reassurance text legible against your header background, and keep it small so it supports rather than overshadows the progress bar.

guides.name: Screen field: Header icon settings
guides.userNeed: Know what "Header icon settings" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Header icon settings
sections.description: Controls the optional header icon shown next to the progress bar — its image (upload or URL), placement relative to the label, scale mode, width, height, corner rounding, and padding. Off by default. Turn it on only to reinforce branding in the header, and keep the icon small so it doesn't crowd the progress bar or the Back and Skip buttons.

guides.name: Screen field: Main button label
guides.userNeed: Know what "Main button label" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Main button label
sections.description: The text on your main call-to-action button — the one that moves visitors to the next screen. Make it a short, specific verb phrase tied to the action (Continue, Get my plan, Subscribe) rather than a generic word; clear, benefit-led labels lift click-through on a paid landing page. This text can be translated per language.

guides.name: Screen field: Main button text style
guides.userNeed: Know what "Main button text style" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Main button text style
sections.description: Typography for the main button label — font, weight, size, color, and alignment. Leave it on the theme defaults for a consistent look; bump the weight or size, or switch color, only when the label is hard to read against the button fill. Applies to the label in every language.

guides.name: Screen field: Main button shape and fill
guides.userNeed: Know what "Main button shape and fill" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Main button shape and fill
sections.description: Sets the main button's look — background color, border, corner radius, height, inner padding, and a full-width toggle. For an ad landing page keep it full-width and high-contrast so it reads as the obvious next step. The Visibility toggle hides the button entirely; only hide it when the screen forces a choice first, and never hide both buttons.

guides.name: Screen field: Gradient on the main button
guides.userNeed: Know what "Gradient on the main button" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Gradient on the main button
sections.description: An optional color gradient layered over the button's solid fill — set start and end colors, the angle, extra color stops, and an optional moving shimmer. Leave it off for a clean flat look; turn it on to make the call-to-action pop against a busy background. Keep enough contrast that the label stays easy to read.

guides.name: Screen field: Shadow under the main button
guides.userNeed: Know what "Shadow under the main button" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Shadow under the main button
sections.description: An optional drop shadow beneath the button, with control over its color, blur, and vertical drop. A soft shadow lifts the call-to-action off the page so it feels tappable; keep it subtle (low blur, small offset) so it looks intentional rather than heavy. Leave it off if your theme is flat.

guides.name: Screen field: Motion on the main button
guides.userNeed: Know what "Motion on the main button" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Motion on the main button
sections.description: Optional animation for the call-to-action — pulse, glow, bounce, scale, fade-in, slide-up and more, plus an opacity control. A gentle pulse or glow can draw the eye and lift taps; save attention-grabbing effects for your key conversion screen and avoid stacking several. Leave it off for a calm, professional feel.

guides.name: Screen field: Icon on the main button
guides.userNeed: Know what "Icon on the main button" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Icon on the main button
sections.description: An optional icon next to the label — choose start or end placement, size, corner radius, and spacing, and how it fits its box (fit shows the whole icon, fill crops to cover). A small leading arrow or lock icon can reinforce the action; keep it in the same color family as the label. Leave it empty for a clean text-only button.

guides.name: Screen field: Secondary button label
guides.userNeed: Know what "Secondary button label" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Secondary button label
sections.description: Text for the optional second button — use it for a side path like Skip, Maybe later, or Restore purchase, never your main goal. On funnel steps an easy escape route can cost conversions, so leave it empty unless you genuinely need the alternative; on a paywall a low-key secondary is fine.

guides.name: Screen field: Secondary button text style
guides.userNeed: Know what "Secondary button text style" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Secondary button text style
sections.description: Typography for the secondary button label — font, weight, size, color, and alignment. Style it deliberately quieter than the main button (lighter weight, muted color) so your primary call-to-action stays the obvious choice. Leave it on theme defaults unless the hierarchy looks off.

guides.name: Screen field: Secondary button shape and fill
guides.userNeed: Know what "Secondary button shape and fill" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Secondary button shape and fill
sections.description: Sets the secondary button's look — background, border, corner radius, height, padding, and a full-width toggle. Give it lower visual weight than the main button (an outline or transparent fill works well) so it doesn't compete with your call-to-action. The Visibility toggle hides it; never hide both the primary and secondary buttons.

guides.name: Screen field: Gradient on the secondary button
guides.userNeed: Know what "Gradient on the secondary button" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Gradient on the secondary button
sections.description: An optional color gradient over the secondary button's solid fill (start/end colors, angle, stops, optional shimmer). Usually leave this off — a gradient draws attention, which you want on your main call-to-action, not the side path. Turn it on only if a flat secondary clashes with your theme.

guides.name: Screen field: Shadow under the secondary button
guides.userNeed: Know what "Shadow under the secondary button" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Shadow under the secondary button
sections.description: An optional drop shadow under the secondary button (color, blur, vertical drop). Keep it lighter than the main button's shadow, or off entirely, so the secondary stays visually subordinate to your call-to-action.

guides.name: Screen field: Motion on the secondary button
guides.userNeed: Know what "Motion on the secondary button" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Motion on the secondary button
sections.description: Adds optional movement to the secondary (lower-priority) button, such as pulse, glow, or bounce, plus an opacity control to fade it. Leave this off by default. Animation draws the eye, so reserve it for your main button only; making the alternative path move competes with your primary call to action and typically lowers conversions.

guides.name: Screen field: Icon on the secondary button
guides.userNeed: Know what "Icon on the secondary button" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Icon on the secondary button
sections.description: An optional icon on the secondary button — placement (start or end), size, corner radius, spacing, and how it fits its box (fit shows the whole icon, fill crops to cover). Usually leave it empty so the secondary stays understated; add one only when it clarifies the action, like a back arrow for Go back.

guides.name: Screen field: What Fills The Background
guides.userNeed: Know what "What Fills The Background" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: What Fills The Background
sections.description: Chooses what sits behind your content: a solid color, a photo, or a video clip, and reveals the matching control below. Defaults to a solid color. Use solid for clean question screens, a photo for emotive intro screens, and video only for short high-impact openers, since heavy video slows loading and can lose paid-ad visitors.

guides.name: Screen field: Solid Background Fill
guides.userNeed: Know what "Solid Background Fill" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Solid Background Fill
sections.description: Sets the single color behind the whole screen when the background is a solid color. Defaults to white. Match it to your theme and ad creative, and keep it high-contrast against your text and buttons so everything stays easy to read on a phone.

guides.name: Screen field: Full-Screen Background Photo
guides.userNeed: Know what "Full-Screen Background Photo" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Full-Screen Background Photo
sections.description: Uploads an image that fills the screen background when the background is set to Photo. It scales to cover the whole screen, so edges can get cropped on different phone sizes, keep your focal point centered. If you put text on top, choose a darker or dimmed image so your copy stays readable.

guides.name: Screen field: Full-Screen Background Video
guides.userNeed: Know what "Full-Screen Background Video" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Full-Screen Background Video
sections.description: Uploads a short clip that fills the screen background when the background is set to Video Clip; it loops on its own. Keep it brief and lightweight, large videos slow the first load and can lose paid-ad visitors before they engage. Make sure any text over it stays readable across the looping frames.

guides.name: Screen field: Tint The Phone's Top Bar
guides.userNeed: Know what "Tint The Phone's Top Bar" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Tint The Phone's Top Bar
sections.description: Sets the color of the surrounding system bars on web funnels, the strip at the top showing time and battery, and the bottom address bar. Leave it unset for almost every screen so it inherits your onboarding default. Set a color only when you want the phone's frame to blend into a full-bleed background for a seamless look.

guides.name: Screen field: Your main headline
guides.userNeed: Know what "Your main headline" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Your main headline
sections.description: The title is the biggest, first thing a visitor reads, so it carries most of the weight on whether they keep going. Turn it on, then write one short benefit-led line, like an ad headline rather than a sentence. Type @ to drop in an earlier answer (for example @user_goal) so it feels personal, and style it under the gear icon below.

guides.name: Screen field: Write the headline text
guides.userNeed: Know what "Write the headline text" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Write the headline text
sections.description: This is where you type the actual headline; keep it short and benefit-driven. Type @ to pull in a visitor's earlier answer (such as @user_goal) for personalization, add a link inside the text with @link, or insert a countdown with @countdown to create urgency on offer screens. If your funnel runs in more than one language, text is saved per language, so switch language before editing each translation.

guides.name: Screen field: Title look and emphasis
guides.userNeed: Know what "Title look and emphasis" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Title look and emphasis
sections.description: Override how the headline looks — font, size, weight, color, alignment, and an optional highlight behind the text. By default it inherits your project theme, which keeps every screen consistent, so most funnels never need to touch this. Override only when one screen needs extra punch, like a bigger color headline on your hero.

guides.name: Screen field: Space around the title
guides.userNeed: Know what "Space around the title" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Space around the title
sections.description: Adds empty space on each side of the title (top, right, bottom, left) so it isn't cramped against the screen edges or the text below. Leave it at the theme default unless the title feels too tight or too far from the next element. Increase a side to give it room, or decrease to pull elements closer together.

guides.name: Screen field: The line under your title
guides.userNeed: Know what "The line under your title" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: The line under your title
sections.description: The subtitle is the supporting line beneath your title; use it to expand the promise, add proof, or hint at what happens next. Turn it on and keep it to one short sentence; it shows smaller and lighter than the title by default so the headline stays dominant. Like the title, you can personalize it with @ variables. Skip it on screens where the title already says everything.

guides.name: Screen field: Write the subtitle text
guides.userNeed: Know what "Write the subtitle text" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Write the subtitle text
sections.description: Type the supporting line that sits under your title here, one short sentence that reinforces the offer or tells the visitor what comes next. The same shortcuts work as in the title: type @ to insert an earlier answer, @link to add a clickable link, or @countdown for urgency. If your funnel is multilingual, text is saved per language, so switch language before editing each translation.

guides.name: Screen field: Subtitle look and emphasis
guides.userNeed: Know what "Subtitle look and emphasis" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Subtitle look and emphasis
sections.description: Change how the subtitle looks — font, size, weight, color, alignment, and an optional background — styled separately from the title so you can tune each one. By default it inherits your theme (usually smaller and lighter than the title), which works for most funnels. Override only when a specific screen needs different emphasis.

guides.name: Screen field: Space around the subtitle
guides.userNeed: Know what "Space around the subtitle" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: Space around the subtitle
sections.description: Adds empty space on each side of the subtitle, controlling the gap above it (to the title) and below it (to what follows). Leave it at the theme default unless the subtitle feels crowded. Increase the top value to separate it from the title, or reduce spacing to tighten the whole headline group.

guides.name: Screen field: The featured image up top
guides.userNeed: Know what "The featured image up top" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: The featured image up top
sections.description: The hero is the large featured image at the top of a headline or wheel-picker screen, the picture that sells the screen at a glance. Turn it on, then upload a file or paste an image URL. Pick a high-quality, on-message visual (product, result, or lifestyle shot); on a paid landing page it is often the first thing a visitor sees. Sizing and position are set just below.

guides.name: Screen field: The hero image itself
guides.userNeed: Know what "The hero image itself" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: The hero image itself
sections.description: Pick the actual hero image: upload a file from your computer or paste a direct image URL, then check the preview thumbnail. Use a high-resolution JPG or PNG so it stays crisp on large screens — uploads are optimized automatically for fast loading. To change it later, just upload or paste a new source here.

guides.name: Screen field: How the image fills its box
guides.userNeed: Know what "How the image fills its box" controls and when to adjust it while editing a screen.

sections.title: How the image fills its box
sections.description: Sets how your image fits its box: Aspect Fit shows the whole image with no cropping (you may see empty bars at the sides), Aspect Fill crops the edges so it fully covers the box, Scale to Fill stretches it (can look distorted, avoid for photos), and Tile repeats it as a pattern.
